Japanese Menu Words: Read More Than “Sushi”

Menus are not tests. They are clues arranged by cooking method.

The most useful Japanese menu vocabulary describes how food is prepared. Once you recognize those building blocks, a menu stops being a wall of kanji. お品書きおしながき (oshinagaki · menu) is the formal word you may see in a restaurant; menu is also widely understood.

Cooking words

焼きやき (yaki · grilled / cooked) appears in yakitori (grilled chicken), okonomiyaki, and yakizakana (grilled fish). 揚げあげ (age · fried) appears in karaage and agemono. Mushi means steamed, yude boiled, and nama raw or fresh. These pieces may appear before or after the ingredient.

The meal formats

定食ていしょく (teishoku · set meal) usually includes a main dish, rice, soup, and pickles. Don means a bowl of rice topped with something: oyakodon has chicken and egg, gyuudon beef. Mori-awase is an assortment, while tabehoudai means all-you-can-eat.

Ingredients worth recognizing

The same few words appear across many menus. Niku is meat, sakana fish, and yasai vegetables. Tori means chicken, buta pork, and gyuu beef. Miso is fermented soybean paste, shio is salt, and tare is a prepared sauce. If you see gohan, it may mean cooked rice or a meal in general; context does the work.

Menus also signal serving style. Hiyashi means chilled, atsumori means hot noodles served hot, and kake indicates broth poured over noodles. Kakiage is a mixed vegetable-and-seafood fritter, while shio-yaki means grilled with salt rather than a sweet soy glaze. Learning these pieces lets you choose by texture and seasoning, not only by photographs.

When a menu lists shun no osusume, it is pointing to the chef’s seasonal recommendation. That phrase is useful because it invites the staff to explain. A good question is kore wa donna aji desu ka? (“What kind of flavor is this?”). Japanese restaurant vocabulary becomes much easier once you treat the menu as a conversation starter.

Specials and uncertainty

季節限定きせつげんてい (kisetsu gentei · seasonal limited) means the item is available for a season or while supplies last. Osusume is the recommendation. If a word is unfamiliar, point and ask kore wa nan desu ka? The answer may be a miniature food lesson, and staff are used to this question.

Sources & further reading

Photographs help, but do not let them become your only strategy. Cover the English description and guess from the cooking word first. Then compare your guess with the picture or ask the staff. This turns an ordinary lunch into repeated, low-pressure reading practice. After a few visits, yaki, age, mushi, and nama start to feel like familiar prefixes rather than isolated vocabulary.

Japanese-language sources — what Japanese readers read about this, not what's written for visitors.

  • 定食 — Japanese Wikipedia
